article.title: OpenAI Just Raised $11 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation, Below the $1.4 Trillion It First Sought - 24/7 Wall St.
article.text:
Investing
OpenAI Just Raised $11 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation, Below the $1.4 Trillion It First Sought
By Omor Ibne Ehsan
Published November 7, 2026, 8:38am ET · 3 min read
𝕏
f
© 24/7 Wall St.
About $11 billion in new money reached OpenAI’s accounts by Friday, November 6, 2026, people familiar with the deal said. That cash is the first part of a round priced at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, a figure the company’s CFO, Sarah Friar, confirmed in a TV interview. OpenAI declined to comment on the funding.
Press reports said OpenAI first set out to raise $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Two investors put the first ask at $1.5 trillion. Friar challenged that account on air, saying the higher figure started with a media report and never came from OpenAI.
Whichever starting point you accept. The round ended up smaller and cheaper after AI stocks sold off, even as OpenAI says its business is accelerating. That gap affects shareholders of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) and NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) because both depend on OpenAI’s ability to fund its plans.
Cash Wired Versus Cash Promised
The closed amount covers about 37% of the original target. SoftBank and Abu Dhabi’s MGX took part in the round.
The rest could lift the total to as much as $20 billion, and a separate report put the follow-on at up to another $9 billion. That second portion has not closed. Lead investors, terms, and use of proceeds were not disclosed.
Friar called the price almost 50% above March, when OpenAI raised $122 billion at $852 billion. The implied step-up is roughly 46.7%, but treat it as approximate, because her figure is pre-money and March’s basis is unclear.
Growth Claims Meet a Tighter Market
Friar said OpenAI’s business grew 70% quarter over quarter in the third quarter, its enterprise business doubled, and revenue splits about 50% each between consumer and enterprise. She cited 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users and an ads run rate of $1 billion by August.
She gave no revenue dollar figures. Asked about the election, she said, “The demand for AI is real.”
Investors still paid less than the earliest reported asking price. Rival Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq in mid-November. Some investors now value it at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion in earlier expectations.
Microsoft Feels This Through GAAP Earnings
Microsoft closed at $530.61, down 0.99%, for a market value of $3.94 trillion. The funding report came out around the close, so that move had other causes.
Gains on the OpenAI stake added $207 million to GAAP net income in the September quarter, compared with $3.1 billion in net losses a year earlier. A smaller valuation increase reduces future gains on the stake, although that is minor next to 48% Azure growth.
NVIDIA Depends on This Money Flowing
NVIDIA rose 2.78% to $186.64 as chip stocks rallied, and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) added 0.78%. NVIDIA is still down 21.4% over one month.
NVIDIA has said OpenAI’s existing and planned commitments add up to about 12 gigawatts of its compute. Management also said frontier labs “are growing faster than what their balance sheets and credit profiles can support.” A round that fills in stages shows that strain.
What OpenAI’s Smaller Round Means for AI Stock Investors
The optimistic view is that demand still exceeds supply. Microsoft says it has more demand than capacity, and NVIDIA guided to $108.0 billion in third-quarter revenue.
The bearish argument depends on financing. Private valuations can drop further, the second portion may close below full size, and a weak Anthropic debut could pull both labs’ valuations down.
Microsoft looks less exposed to OpenAI’s funding pace than NVIDIA, because OpenAI affects its accounting gains far more than the cloud business behind its earnings. NVIDIA is more exposed to how well the labs can raise money.
Two milestones will test this view: whether OpenAI’s round reaches $20 billion, and whether NVIDIA meets its guidance…

article.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic
article.text:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

article.title: Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment — LoreKit blog
article.text:
All posts
Agent memory needs its OpenTelemetry moment
Every agent tool stores memory in its own shape, and every week someone builds another one. None of them can read the others. Observability had the same problem until OpenTelemetry gave everyone one data model to share. A tour of today's memory formats, the proposals that already exist, and what a shared spec could look like.
Mads Thines·November 7, 2026·7 min read
Count the memory formats on your machine
List every place your coding tools keep something they "remember". A typical setup today:
an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md in most repos, and .cursor/rules/*.mdc in a few
an agent writing files to a /memories directory through Anthropic's memory tool
Copilot keeping facts about each repo on GitHub's side
a memory MCP server keeping a JSONL knowledge graph
That's four different shapes, and none of them can read the others. A lesson your CI agent learns stays in whatever wrote it. Your editor agent can't read it, and neither can the next tool you try.
Each format is reasonable on its own. Together, they rebuild the same small idea again and again: a note an agent left for its future self, stored at some address, true for a while.
And the list keeps growing. Browse r/ClaudeAI, r/LocalLLaMA or r/cursor and you'll find a steady stream of "I built a memory layer for my agent" posts, each with its own storage, its own schema and its own MCP tools. That's good evidence the problem is real: people keep hitting it badly enough to build something. But every new solution adds one more format that nothing else can read. The problem isn't a missing tool. It's a missing agreement, and that only comes from the community working on it together.
I build one of these tools, LoreKit, which is open source. This isn't a pitch that LoreKit has solved memory. Its format is one proposal among several, with gaps of its own. The point is that this is the moment to agree on a shared shape, and that another field has already shown how.
We've seen this before
Before 2019, every observability vendor shipped its own agent, its own instrumentation library and its own data format. Switching vendors meant instrumenting your code again. Two open projects, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, tried to fix that and competed with each other too.
In 2019 they merged into OpenTelemetry. What mattered was what the vendors agreed to stop competing on:
A data model: what a span, a metric and a log record are.
Semantic conventions: shared names like service.name and http.*.
A protocol: OTLP, one way to send the data.
Reference implementations: shared SDKs and the Collector.
Vendors kept competing on what they do with the data: storage, querying, analysis. Users instrument once. I work with OpenTelemetry every day at Dash0, and that agreement is why a whole ecosystem of tools can read each other's data.
The same four layers. Observability agreed on them and competes on what happens after the data arrives. Agent memory has plenty of implementations, but nothing agreed underneath them.
Agent memory is where observability was before 2019. The timing is good: the formats are young enough to change, and there's already a neutral home for agent standards. MCP and AGENTS.md both sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.
A tour of the shapes
These change quickly, so treat the details as a snapshot from late 2026.

Google Antigravity for Knowledge Work
The Antigravity Team
·Nov 9, 2026·4 min read
Share on XShare on BlueskyShare on LinkedIn
As the adoption of Google Antigravity has scaled, we’ve seen people bring Antigravity far more than code. Alongside software engineering, more and more daily sessions center on deep research, data analysis, drafting documents and presentations, prototyping designs, and automating everyday workflows. We’ve seen this exact same pull inside Google, where tens of thousands of Googlers outside software engineering (across sales, finance, legal, product, design, research, marketing, and operations) now rely on Antigravity every week alongside engineers to get their work done.
Software development at the core, built with every role in mind
We are in the business of helping the world deliver value through products and research. No matter what you are working on, the underlying logic and systems eventually need to be built, and that requires software development. That’s why software development is, and will remain, at the core of what Antigravity enables.
But actually delivering value never happens in a silo. It requires every role—engineering, product, design, data, science, operations, and go-to-market—working together with a common language, shared context, and mutual understanding. And the exact same agentic capabilities forged on complex software engineering (multi-step reasoning, working directly across local folders and connected tools, orchestrating subagents and plugins, and iterating on rich artifacts) are what make an agent genuinely useful for rigorous knowledge work, too.
Supporting knowledge work shouldn’t mean pointing non-developers to a watered-down experience, nor should it mean forcing everyone to navigate Git worktrees, terminal panes, and line-by-line code diffs just to collaborate with an agent. That’s why Antigravity is built with everyone doing knowledge work in mind, and why today we are launching a new Knowledge Work user experience in Google Antigravity to support both software engineering and broader knowledge work.
One Antigravity agent, tailored to how you work
While Antigravity’s default UI was built around repositories, terminals, and code diffs, you can now choose between two interface layouts in the Antigravity App: Knowledge Work and Software Engineering. Both layouts run the exact same Antigravity agent, with full access to frontier models, local files, plugins, skills, rules, custom agents, and MCP servers, so these visual changes make Antigravity more approachable and intuitive for professional knowledge work without giving up any underlying capability.
Alongside interface layouts, we’ve rolled out an updated role-based onboarding flow for new users. When signing in for the first time, you can select what best describes your work (starting with Software Engineering, Knowledge Work, Data & Analytics, Science, or Design) to automatically tailor your starting interface layout, starter prompts, and recommended…

Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting.
